---
title: 'Sign-In For Native, Desktop And CLI Apps'
description: 'Sign users in to desktop apps, CLIs and other native apps through the Seamless Auth OpenID Provider the RFC 8252 way (public client, system browser, PKCE, loopback or private-use redirects, keychain storage), and give a desktop app a backend with verify-only tokens, step-up and account notices, with runnable Electron and CLI examples.'

import { Aside } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'

Desktop apps, CLIs and developer tools sign users in through the Seamless Auth
[OpenID Provider](/build/openid-provider) as **public clients**, following RFC 8252 (OAuth 2.0 for
Native Apps). The app opens the user's system browser on the hosted sign-in page, the user signs in
there (with a passkey or any other enabled method), and the browser hands an authorization code back
to the app through a loopback address or a private-use URI scheme. The app exchanges the code with
PKCE. It never sees the user's credentials and never holds a client secret.

Read [Use Seamless Auth As An OpenID Provider](/build/openid-provider) first for the edge service,
the registry and the token model. This page covers what is different for native apps.

<Aside type="note" title="Status">
  Sign-in ships in v0.21 with the OpenID Provider, including sign-out and the device authorization
  grant for CLIs on machines without a browser. Part of [An App With Its Own
  Backend](#an-app-with-its-own-backend) is not released: account notices through a client link need
  Seamless Auth API v0.23.0, which is not published yet. See [Versions](#versions). So does `seamless
  profile login` through the provider, described in [A Runnable CLI
  Example](#a-runnable-cli-example).
</Aside>

---

## The Rules

1. **Register a public client.** A native app cannot keep a secret: anything in the binary can be
   extracted. A public client authenticates with PKCE alone, has no secret and no keys, and cannot
   use `client_credentials`. The registry refuses any other combination.
2. **Use the system browser, never an embedded webview.** A webview lets the app read what the user
   types, and the user cannot tell a real sign-in page from a copy. Open the authorization URL in the
   default browser (or `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on macOS and iOS, Custom Tabs on Android).
3. **Use PKCE with `S256`.** Every client must. The edge refuses `plain` and requests without PKCE.
4. **Receive the code on a loopback redirect or a private-use scheme.** See the next section.
5. **Keep tokens in the OS credential store**: the macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, or the
   Secret Service API (GNOME Keyring, KWallet) on Linux. Not a plain file, not an environment
   variable. See [Keep Tokens In The OS Credential Store](#keep-tokens-in-the-os-credential-store).

---

## Redirect URIs

A public client registers its redirect URIs like any other application. The registry and the edge
accept three forms:

| Form                | Example                       | Matching                                                                   |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| IPv4 loopback       | `http://127.0.0.1/callback`   | Any port at request time. Scheme, host and path must match exactly.       |
| IPv6 loopback       | `http://[::1]/callback`       | Any port at request time. Scheme, host and path must match exactly.       |
| Private-use scheme  | `com.example.desk:/callback`  | Exact. The scheme must be in reverse domain form.                          |
| Claimed `https` URL | `https://desk.example.com/cb` | Exact, port included. For apps that claim links (universal or app links). |

An application with a loopback or private-use redirect is reported as `applicationType: native`.

### Loopback on any port (RFC 8252 section 7.3)

Register the loopback URI **without a port**. At sign-in, the app listens on whatever port the OS
gives it and sends that port in `redirect_uri`:

```text
registered:   http://127.0.0.1/callback
requested:    http://127.0.0.1:53124/callback     accepted
requested:    http://[::1]:61000/callback         accepted if http://[::1]/callback is registered
requested:    http://127.0.0.1:53124/other        refused (path differs)
requested:    https://127.0.0.1:53124/callback    refused (scheme differs)
requested:    http://127.0.0.2:53124/callback     refused (host differs)
requested:    http://localhost:53124/callback     refused (localhost)
```

Bind the listener to the loopback interface only (`127.0.0.1` or `::1`), never to all interfaces.
The port exception applies only to these loopback URIs. A web application's `https` redirect never
matches on a different port.

### Why not `localhost`

`localhost` is refused as a redirect host, at registration and at sign-in (RFC 8252 section 8.3).
The name can resolve to an address other than the loopback interface, or to the IPv6 address when
the app listens on IPv4. Use the literal `127.0.0.1` or `[::1]`.

### Private-use schemes (RFC 8252 section 7.1)

A private-use scheme must be in reverse domain form, a name with at least one dot that you control,
such as `com.example.desk:/callback`. The dot keeps out `javascript:`, `data:` and every other scheme
a browser acts on. Register the scheme with the OS so the browser hands the redirect to your app.
Any app can claim the same scheme on most platforms, which is why PKCE is required: an app that
intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier.

## A CLI Example

A complete loopback sign-in for a Node CLI, with [`openid-client`](https://github.com/panva/openid-client).
Register the client first:

```bash
seamless clients create "Example CLI" --public --first-party \
  --redirect-uri http://127.0.0.1/callback \
  --grants authorization_code,refresh_token
```

```ts
import { createServer } from 'node:http'
import { once } from 'node:events'
import open from 'open'
import * as oidc from 'openid-client'

const config = await oidc.discovery(
  new URL('https://login.example.com'),
  'CLI_CLIENT_ID',
  undefined,
  oidc.None(),
)

// Port 0: the OS picks a free port on the loopback interface.
const server = createServer()
server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1')
await once(server, 'listening')
const { port } = server.address() as { port: number }
const redirectUri = `http://127.0.0.1:${port}/callback`

const verifier = oidc.randomPKCECodeVerifier()
const state = oidc.randomState()
const url = oidc.buildAuthorizationUrl(config, {
  redirect_uri: redirectUri,
  scope: 'openid offline_access',
  prompt: 'consent',
  code_challenge: await oidc.calculatePKCECodeChallenge(verifier),
  code_challenge_method: 'S256',
  state,
})

await open(url.href)

const [request, response] = await once(server, 'request')
const callbackUrl = new URL(request.url, redirectUri)
response.end('Signed in. You can close this tab.')
server.close()

const tokens = await oidc.authorizationCodeGrant(config, callbackUrl, {
  pkceCodeVerifier: verifier,
  expectedState: state,
})
// Store tokens.refresh_token in the OS credential store.
```

`offline_access` with `prompt=consent` gets a refresh token, so the CLI does not send the user back
to the browser every time the access token expires. See [Refresh tokens](/build/openid-provider#refresh-tokens).

---

## Keep Tokens In The OS Credential Store

- **The refresh token** goes in the OS credential store and nowhere else. If the store is locked or
  absent, sign-in should fail and say so. Do not fall back to a file.
- **The access token** stays in memory. It is short-lived and cheap to refresh.
- **The ID token** stays in memory too, for `id_token_hint` on sign-out. A refresh returns a new one.
- **One refresher at a time.** An app with several processes (a tray helper, a CLI, the main window)
  refreshes through one of them, or behind a lock. In Electron, `app.requestSingleInstanceLock()`
  and one in-flight refresh in the main process cover the app itself.
- **Save before use.** Store a rotated refresh token before using the new access token, so a crash
  cannot leave the app holding a spent one.
- **The renderer never sees a token.** In Electron or Tauri, keep tokens in the native process and
  give the page the results of calls, so script running in the page has nothing to take.

A library that reaches the store directly is the simplest route. The example uses
[`@napi-rs/keyring`](https://github.com/Brooooooklyn/keyring-node), with
`{ linux: { store: 'secret-service' } }`: by default it falls back on Linux to the kernel keyring,
which is memory only, so the user would be signed out at every reboot. Two things that look like the
same choice are not, as checked on 2026-11-04:

- [`keytar`](https://github.com/atom/node-keytar), the older Node library, is archived on GitHub.
- Electron's [`safeStorage`](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/safe-storage) encrypts data
  for you to store yourself, and it is not a credential store. On Linux with no secret store, it
  falls back to a hardcoded password, and `safeStorage.getSelectedStorageBackend()` returns
  `basic_text`. If you use it anyway, check that and refuse.

---

## Refresh, API Tokens And Sign-Out

- **Refresh.** Refresh tokens rotate on every use. Save the new one each time, before using the new
  access token. A refresh token used twice revokes the grant and ends the user's Seamless session,
  so two processes of the same app must not refresh with one token at the same time. `acr`, `amr`
  and `auth_time` on the new access token are the session's, so a step-up survives a refresh.
- **Tokens for your API.** Ask for a token for a named API with `resource=<identifier>` on the
  authorization request, using a resource the application is linked to. The access token is an RFC
  9068 JWT whose `aud` is that API. See
  [Access tokens for your API](/build/openid-provider#access-tokens-for-your-api).
- **Signing out of the app.** Revoke the refresh token at `/token/revocation` (a public client sends
  its `client_id`), then delete the stored tokens. That ends this app's grant only. The user stays
  signed in to Seamless in the browser and in their other apps. An access token already issued
  keeps working at a backend that verifies tokens locally until it expires, so keep access token
  lifetimes short ([`accessTokenTtlSeconds`](/build/openid-provider#refresh-tokens)).
- **Signing out of Seamless.** To end the user's Seamless session too, revoke and delete the tokens,
  then open the [end session URL](/build/openid-provider#rp-initiated-logout) in the system
  browser, where the Seamless session cookie lives. The hosted page asks the user to confirm. To
  bring the user back to the app, register a `post_logout_redirect_uri` and pass it with a `state`.
  A loopback URI registered for a native application matches on any port, as a redirect URI does,
  so the listener can use a port the OS picks. Every other form is matched exactly.

```ts
const logoutUrl = oidc.buildEndSessionUrl(config, {
  id_token_hint: tokens.id_token!,
  post_logout_redirect_uri: 'com.example.desk:/signed-out',
  state: oidc.randomState(),
})
await open(logoutUrl.href)
```

---

## CLIs Without A Browser: Device Authorization Grant

A CLI on a server, over SSH or in a container cannot open a browser for the loopback flow. The
device authorization grant (RFC 8628) covers it: the CLI prints a code, and the user approves it in
a browser on any other device. It is available to first-party applications with the device flow
on:

```bash
seamless clients update <id> --device-flow
```

A CLI can then offer both flows, the loopback flow when a browser is at hand and the device flow
when it is not:

```ts
const device = await oidc.initiateDeviceAuthorization(config, {
  scope: 'openid offline_access',
})
console.error(`Open ${device.verification_uri} and enter ${device.user_code}`)
const tokens = await oidc.pollDeviceAuthorizationGrant(config, device)
// Store tokens.refresh_token in the OS credential store.
```

- **Codes** are 8 characters (`BCDF-GHJK`), live 10 minutes, and work once.
- **Polling** waits `interval` (5 seconds). A poll that comes too soon gets `slow_down`; `openid-client`
  backs off for you.
- **Approval always signs in again**, even in a browser already signed in to Seamless, after a page
  that names the app and warns the user to continue only for a device they started.
- **No `acr`.** Device tokens never carry `acr`, after a refresh too, and `acr_values` or `max_age`
  on a device request is refused. Do not use the device flow where an API needs `phr` or `phrh`.
- **An expired code** currently answers `invalid_grant`, not RFC 8628's `expired_token`
  ([seamless-auth-api#542](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/issues/542)). Treat both
  the same: stop polling and start again.

The full flow, poll answers and the verification page are in
[Device authorization grant](/build/openid-provider#device-authorization-grant).

---

## Why Passkeys Run On The Hosted Page

A passkey is bound to a relying party ID, the instance's `rpid` (for example `example.com`), and a
browser only offers it on a page whose origin is that domain or a subdomain of it. The hosted
sign-in page runs on the provider's issuer (for example `https://login.example.com`), which the API
requires to sit under `rpid`, so every passkey the user already has works there.

An app's own webview cannot do the same. Its origin is `tauri://localhost`, `app://`, `file://` or
similar, which can never match `rpid`, so the WebAuthn ceremony fails, and an embedded webview
cannot reach the passkeys synced to the user's browser or phone in any case. Sending the user to
the system browser keeps passkeys, saved sessions and any security keys working, and keeps the app
out of the credential path.

The same page handles step-up. When a backend asks for a recent passkey, the app opens the system
browser again, and the user confirms on the hosted page with the session they already have.

---

## An App With Its Own Backend

Most desktop apps call their own API. The app holds the user's tokens and nothing else, and the
backend trusts a call by verifying its token locally. The auth API stays private, so the app never
reaches it.

```text
desktop app (public client) ──system browser──► login edge ──► auth API (private)
      │  access token, aud = backend resource         ▲              ▲
      ▼                                               │ JWKS         │ notices, client credentials
backend API (resource server) ── verify-only adapter ─┘              │ through a client link
      └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The design is [ADR 0002](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/blob/main/docs/adr/0002-native-and-desktop-apps.md).
Nothing in it is specific to one product.

### Versions

The example was run against the versions in the last column. Anything earlier is unverified, even
where a feature first shipped sooner.

| Piece                                                                     | Needs                                                                                                                      | Run against                                                                                      |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Public client, loopback redirect, PKCE, API tokens, refresh, revocation   | The provider, from v0.21                                                                                                   | Edge image `seamless-auth-oidc-provider:v0.3.0`                                                  |
| `acr`, `amr` and `auth_time` on an access token for a resource            | `@seamless-auth/oidc-provider` 0.3.0                                                                                       | Edge image `v0.3.0`                                                                              |
| Verify-only guards (`createResourceServer`)                               | `@seamless-auth/express` 0.23.0, with the same guards in the Fastify, Next.js, Go, Python and Rust adapters                | `@seamless-auth/express` 0.24.0                                                                  |
| Client links and `clientId` on account notices                            | **Seamless Auth API v0.23.0, which is not published.** API v0.22.0 has no link routes.                                     | The API built from source at [`bcab4d1`](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/commit/bcab4d1b62ebb1f14e9b3eda8297ede01e38962f) |

### Register Three Records

| Record         | Registry entry                                                                                      | Holds                              |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Desktop app    | Application, `clientType: public`, `tokenEndpointAuthMethod: none`, a loopback or private-use URI   | Nothing secret                     |
| Backend client | Application, `clientType: confidential`, `private_key_jwt`, `client_credentials`, notices turned on | A private key, on the backend only |
| Backend API    | Resource, an absolute URI such as `https://api.example.com`, with its scopes                        | Nothing; it names the audience     |

Allow both applications the resource with `PUT /admin/applications/:id/resources`. Then link the
backend client to the desktop app (API v0.23.0) with
`PUT /admin/applications/<backend id>/links/<desktop id>`. A link says the backend acts for that
app. The acting client must be confidential and the linked one public, and both must be first-party
or both third-party. Every write needs a fresh step-up and is audited.

### Verify Tokens In The Backend

Use the verify-only guards of your adapter, as in
[Verify Tokens In Your API](/build/openid-provider#verify-tokens-in-your-api). They check the
signature, `iss`, `aud`, `typ` and `exp` locally, and never call the auth API. One check is yours:
which clients this API serves. The adapter accepts any valid token for the resource, so without
this, another client allowed the same resource could call it. In the example, the backend's own
client credentials token verifies, and this check is what answers it with a 403.

```ts
import { createResourceServer } from '@seamless-auth/express'

const api = createResourceServer({
  issuer: 'https://login.example.com',
  audience: 'https://api.example.com',
})

const clients = new Set(['DESKTOP_CLIENT_ID'])
function requireClient(req, res, next) {
  if (clients.has(req.user.clientId)) return next()
  res.status(403).json({ error: 'client_not_allowed' })
}

app.get('/notes', api.requireAuth(), requireClient, api.requireScope('notes:read'), listNotes)
```

### Require A Recent Passkey On One Route

The backend decides which routes are sensitive. `requireStepUp` answers with the RFC 9470 challenge
until the token shows what the route asks for:

```ts
app.post(
  '/notes/export',
  api.requireAuth(),
  requireClient,
  api.requireScope('notes:read'),
  api.requireStepUp({ acrValues: ['phr'], maxAge: 300 }),
  exportNotes,
)
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="insufficient_user_authentication",
  error_description="A different authentication level is required", acr_values="phr", max_age="300"
```

The app reads the challenge, accepting quoted or bare values, and then:

1. Opens the system browser on a new authorization request with the same `resource` and scopes,
   plus the `acr_values` and `max_age` from the challenge.
2. The user confirms on the hosted page, which offers their passkey on the session they already
   have.
3. The app exchanges the code, stores the new refresh token, and retries the call once.
4. The app revokes the refresh token it replaced. A step-up starts a new grant, so the old one
   would otherwise stay usable until it expires.

`acr` says how strong and `max_age` says how recent, so a route that needs a passkey within five
minutes asks for both. The challenge comes back once `auth_time` is older than `max_age`. Do not
use the device flow for such a route, since device tokens never carry `acr`.

### Send A Notice Through The Client Link

Users sign in to the desktop app, so the backend's own client holds no grants and could reach
nobody. A link fixes that. The backend gets a client credentials token with its own key and names
the desktop app in `clientId`. The template names the app the user knows, not the backend.

<Aside type="caution" title="Needs API v0.23.0">
  `clientId` and the link routes are not in a published API yet. On API v0.22.0, an application can
  only send to users who hold a grant with that same application. See
  [Account Notices](/build/openid-provider#account-notices-from-an-application).
</Aside>

```ts
const { access_token } = await oidc.clientCredentialsGrant(backendConfig, {
  resource: 'https://login.example.com/seamless',
  scope: 'notices:send',
})

await fetch('https://auth-api.internal.example.com/applications/account-notices', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${access_token}`, 'content-type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    userId: req.user.id,
    clientId: 'DESKTOP_CLIENT_ID',
    subject: 'Your notes export is ready',
    text: 'The export you asked for is ready in the app.',
  }),
})
```

A user token cannot send a notice, and neither can a public client, which cannot use
`client_credentials`. The backend's private key never ships in the app.

## A Runnable Desktop Example

[`examples/native-desktop`](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-docs/tree/main/examples/native-desktop)
is an Electron app and an Express backend that do everything on this page against a local instance:
system browser sign-in, a loopback redirect on a port the OS picks, PKCE, the OS keychain, refresh,
sign-out with revocation, a token for a named API, a route that answers the RFC 9470 challenge until
the user steps up, and a notice through a client link. Its README has the steps, and it runs on the
[local recipe](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/tree/main/local).

CI runs it end to end on a schedule, with a virtual authenticator in Chromium standing in for the
user's passkey and default browser. That covers the flow and the keychain. It does not cover a real
browser being opened by the OS, a physical authenticator, or Windows. The README lists exactly what
it does and does not check.

---

## A Runnable CLI Example

[`examples/native-cli`](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-docs/tree/main/examples/native-cli)
is a small standalone CLI that does the client side of this page against a local instance: `login`
through the system browser with a loopback redirect and PKCE `S256`, `login --device` with the device
grant, refresh, and `logout` with revocation. It is a public client with no secret, and its tokens
are in the OS keychain with no file fallback. It uses nothing new in API v0.23.0, but the
[local recipe](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-oidc-provider/tree/main/local) it runs on
builds that unpublished API from source, for its seed's client links, so it has not been run against
a published API.

A CLI differs from a desktop app in three ways, and each one is easy to get wrong:

- **Every command is a new process.** Memory does not survive between commands, so the example keeps
  the access token in the keychain too, with its expiry. Without that, every command would spend a
  refresh.
- **Commands run at the same time.** A refresh token used twice revokes the grant and ends the user's
  Seamless session, and two commands in a pipeline or in two terminals are enough. So a refresh
  takes a lock that spans processes and reads the keychain again once it holds the lock, because the
  command it waited for has already rotated the token. With the lock removed, the example's check of
  six commands at once fails with the grant revoked.
- **stdout belongs to the result.** Prompts, URLs and errors go to stderr, so
  `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $(notes token)"` works.

`login` also prints the URL it opens, and honours the `BROWSER` environment variable. On a machine
with no browser, the printed hint leads to `--device`.

CI runs it end to end on a schedule, with the real CLI as a child process, the real keychain, and a
virtual authenticator in Chromium standing in for the user's passkey and default browser. That does
not cover a real browser being opened by the OS, a physical authenticator, Windows, a locked
keychain, or a device code that expires. The README lists exactly what it does and does not check.

### Signing In To Seamless With The Seamless CLI

<Aside type="caution" title="Merged, not released">
  What this section describes is merged in
  [seamless-cli#349](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-cli/pull/349), but no published
  `seamless-cli` has it yet, and it needs Seamless Auth API v0.23.0 and the provider edge. API v0.23.0
  is not published. The published CLI (0.27.2) signs in to an instance with an email code.
</Aside>

`seamless profile login` follows the same rules for one more purpose: an operator signing in to an
instance they administer. It differs from the example above in what it keeps. It uses the provider
sign-in once, then exchanges the provider's access token at `POST /sessions/exchange` for a
first-party session, stores that session in the OS keychain, and keeps no token from the provider.

```bash
seamless profile login prod            # system browser, loopback redirect, PKCE S256
seamless profile login prod --device   # the device grant, for a machine with no browser
seamless profile login prod \
  --oidc-issuer https://auth.example.com --client-id <client id>
```

- **The exchange token.** The access token is a single-use `session:exchange` token that lasts 60
  seconds. The CLI never retries an exchange: presenting the token a second time revokes the session
  the first attempt created ([ADR 0003](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/blob/main/docs/adr/0003-native-admin-access.md)).
- **Finding the provider.** Flags win over the saved profile, which wins over `oidcProvider { issuer,
  cliClientId }` on `GET /system-config/public`. So an instance that stops advertising cannot downgrade
  a profile. With no provider anywhere, the CLI uses an email code.
- **Trusting the advertisement.** The CLI reads it only over https or on loopback. An advertised issuer
  on another origin needs the user's confirmation, and without a terminal the CLI stops and asks for
  the flags. Instances cannot set `oidc_cli_client_id` through `seamless config` yet
  ([seamless-cli#351](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-cli/issues/351)), so plan on passing
  `--oidc-issuer` and `--client-id` once. The sign-in saves them to the profile.
- **Device sessions step up.** A session from `--device` must step up with the authenticator app before
  admin and organization commands, reads included, because whoever approved the code may not be
  whoever holds this terminal.
- **The client.** An admin registers a first-party public client with a loopback redirect, with
  session exchange on, and the device grant on for `--device`:

```bash
seamless clients create "Seamless CLI" --public --first-party --auth-method none \
  --redirect-uri http://127.0.0.1/callback --device-flow --session-exchange
```

The session exchange is for first-party admin access, so your own CLI should not copy this part. Copy
the example, and call your API with the provider's token. See the
[CLI reference](/reference/cli-commands#profile) for the flags.

---

## Where DPoP Will Fit

<Aside type="caution" title="Not shipped">
  DPoP ([seamless-auth-api#512](https://github.com/fells-code/seamless-auth-api/issues/512)) and
  device-bound keys do not exist in Seamless Auth yet. This section is the intended direction, and it
  may change.
</Aside>

Today, every token on this page is a bearer token: whoever holds it can use it, which is why the
storage rules above are the protection. DPoP (RFC 9449) binds a token to a key the app holds, so a
stolen token alone would not be enough. When #512 ships, this page should recommend a non-exportable
key in the platform keystore where one exists. On the backend, the verify-only guards already refuse
a sender-constrained token (`cnf`) unless you pass a `confirm` hook, which is where a proof check
would plug in.

---

## What OAuth 2.1 Refuses

The provider is locked to OAuth 2.1 and RFC 9700. These are refused for every client, native or
not (a confidential client can be [opted out of PKCE](/build/openid-provider#pkce-and-nonce-opt-outs), a
public one never):

| Refused                                                       | Answer                                                    |
| ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Implicit and hybrid flows (`response_type=token`, `id_token`) | `unsupported_response_type` or `invalid_request`          |
| PKCE `plain`, or no PKCE on a public client                  | `invalid_request`                                         |
| Resource owner password grant (`grant_type=password`)         | `unsupported_grant_type`                                  |
| A redirect URI that does not match a registered one           | An error page; the code is never sent there               |
| `localhost` or a non-loopback `http` redirect                 | Refused at registration and at sign-in                    |
| A client secret on a public client                            | Refused at registration                                   |
| `client_credentials` for a public client                      | Refused at registration                                   |
| An authorization code redeemed twice                          | `invalid_grant`, and the tokens from the first use are revoked |
| Dynamic client registration                                   | Not offered: applications come only from the registry     |
